author: Mrkol
content: most important thing to understand about git is that it's a persistent storage: commit are never destroyed or modified. You only move around branches/tags which are basically pointers to commits around a huge tree of commits, and the only case in which git destroys commits is when a commit is unreachable through any branch/tag/ref

author: Mrkol
content: it gets much easier to `git` when you internalize this point

author: Mrkol
content: also, each local checkout of a repo contains both local and remote branch-pointers which might be pointing to different commits

author: Mrkol
content: so if you fuck up your local git, the only thing you've actually fucked up is the local master branch pointer usually

author: Mrkol
content: and doing `git reset --hard origin/master` usually fixes everything, which force-moves the pointer to whatever commit the remote master points to

author: Mrkol
content: note that this does NOT delete old commits that you've been previously pointing to and you can return your master to point to them if you want to

author: Mrkol
content: but you have to know the hash, which can be looked up via the history of what master has been pointing to recently `git reflog`

content: so when you do a fork, you actually have 2 remote repositories: your fork (origin) and original repo (upstream)

author: Mrkol
content: and so if upstream gets new commits, you have to somehow update your fork and your local changes w.r.t. those commits

author: Mrkol
content: what I recommend to do is a `git rebase origin/master --onto upstream/master` which takes all the commits in the chain from `origin/master` to `master` and tries to reapply their changes on top of `upstream/master` and create new commits

author: Mrkol
content: (and then move `master` to these new commits)

author: Mrkol
content: then you can force-push your mster to `origin/master` and you're done
